_readme: The client that cannot hold a SuperDocs key.
Antigravity's shipped mcp_config.json documentation defines `command`/`args`/`env` for stdio
and `serverUrl` for SSE. There is no headers field for either. SuperDocs authenticates with
`Authorization: Bearer`, so a working SuperDocs entry cannot be expressed here at all.
Every case therefore ends in `files_unchanged`. That is not a limitation being hidden — it is
the diagnosis, and reporting it plainly is more useful than emitting repair advice that could

cases.name: empty-config-file
cases.description: A freshly installed client. Both mcp_config.json files on the machine this was captured from were 0 bytes.
cases._why: An empty file is not a corrupt one. Reporting 'invalid JSON at line 1, column 1' would be technically true and completely unhelpful — and it would send someone hunting for damage that is not there.

cases.name: server-url-field-is-found
cases.description: A SuperDocs entry using serverUrl. It must be FOUND — a doctor hunting for `url` would report 'no entry' while one sits in front of it.
cases._why: The whole reason the URL field name is registry data rather than the constant 'url'. Three clients so far: url, url, serverUrl.

cases.name: cannot-authenticate-even-when-otherwise-correct
cases.description: A canonical URL, correct in every way the client permits — and still unusable, because there is nowhere to put the key.
cases._why: config.auth-header-missing would be the WRONG finding: it implies adding a header would help, and `--fix` would then be expected to add one to a schema with no such field. The distinction between 'you forgot the header' and 'this client has no headers' is the entire value of the diagnosis.

cases.name: stdio-server
cases.description: A local-process entry, the shape the shipped documentation leads with.
cases._why: stdio is checked BEFORE the cannot-authenticate rule: a stdio server passes its key through env, so the header limitation does not apply to it.

cases.name: host-rule-gateway
cases.description: The host rule still applies here, and takes precedence over the authentication limitation.
cases._why: Ordering matters. Off the canonical host we have no opinion at all — including no opinion about whether the client could authenticate against whatever lives there, which may not need a Bearer key.
